results.question: I put $7,000 into an account and later another $2,000 was counted; what tax would I pay while the extra stays there?

The tax is **1% per month of the highest excess amount in the account during that month**, for every month the excess remains there.

- On a $2,000 excess, that is **$20 per month**.
- For example, if it stays for 3 months, the tax would be **$60**.
- Even if the $2,000 is removed later in the same month it was counted, the 1% tax for that month still applies: **$20**.

CRA says to withdraw the full excess as soon as possible to reduce the monthly tax. If the excess arose while you were also a non-resident of Canada, separate non-resident contribution tax rules can also apply.

This assumes you actually had only $7,000 of TFSA room; the result changes if you had unused room available from earlier years. For your specific records and tax amount, confirm with CRA or a licensed tax professional.

results.question: Do direct transfers to an RRSP affect my RRSP deduction limit, and can I make such a transfer after age 71?

Generally, **a direct transfer to your RRSP does not use or reduce your RRSP deduction limit**. It is not treated as a regular RRSP contribution for deduction-limit purposes. Depending on the type of transfer, you may have to report the amount as income and claim an offsetting deduction on your tax return.

For age 71:

- If you transfer an amount **to your own RRSP**, you must be **71 or younger at the end of the calendar year of the transfer**.
- In the year you turn 71, CRA says you must choose to withdraw your RRSP funds, transfer them to a RRIF, or use them to buy an annuity.
- After December of the year you turn 71, you generally cannot make a transfer to **your own** RRSP. A separate rule may permit contributions to a younger spouse’s or common-law partner’s RRSP if you have available deduction room.

The exact tax reporting and eligibility can depend on where the funds are coming from (for example, an RPP, RRIF, another RRSP, or FHSA). For example, CRA says a **direct FHSA-to-RRSP or RRIF transfer** generally does not affect unused RRSP deduction room, provided the conditions are met.

results.question: When must my jointly owned business report assets held outside Canada, and what value range allows the simpler reporting method?
results.answer:
A jointly owned business that is a **partnership** must file **Form T1135 (Foreign Income Verification Statement)** if the partnership holds **specified foreign property costing more than $100,000**.

The form is due by the earlier of:

- **March 31** after the calendar year in which the partnership’s fiscal period ended; or  
- **Five months after** the end of the partnership’s fiscal period.

The **simplified reporting method (Part A)** is available where the total cost of specified foreign property was **more than $100,000 but less than $250,000 throughout the year**. If the total cost was **$250,000 or more at any time during the year**, the detailed method (Part B) applies.

“Specified foreign property” can include, for example, funds held outside Canada, foreign shares, debts owed by non-residents, foreign insurance policies, and tangible property outside Canada. Property used or held exclusively in an active business is excluded.

This is general CRA information; whether a particular jointly owned business is a partnership and whether its assets qualify as “specified foreign property” can depend on the facts. Consider confirming with a tax professional or the CRA.

results.question: If I put money into this tax-free savings option, take some out, or pay fees, how does that change what I can add later?

- **Putting money in:** Each contribution reduces your available TFSA contribution room immediately, dollar for dollar. This applies across **all** of your TFSAs combined—not separately for each account.

  *Example:* If you withdraw $2,000 in 2026, that $2,000 becomes new contribution room on January 1, 2027. Re-contributing it in 2026 could create an over-contribution unless you already had unused room.

- **Paying fees:** TFSA management fees you pay, and certain fees paid by the TFSA trust (such as investment-counsel fees), **do not change** your available contribution room.

- **Adding room each year:** The Government sets a new annual TFSA dollar limit every January 1. Unused contribution room from earlier years can also carry forward. Contributing more than your available room is an over-contribution and is generally taxed at **1% per month** on the excess.

Because CRA account information is updated only once a year in the spring using the previous year’s transactions, CRA says to use your own records when calculating current available room. For your exact situation, consider confirming with CRA or a licensed advisor.

results.question: On marriage breakdown, when is a direct FHSA-to-FHSA/RRSP/RRIF transfer to a spouse or former partner tax-free, and how is the maximum calculated?

> **minus your excess FHSA amount at that time.**

results.question: Could I qualify as a first-time buyer when opening the account but not meet the requirement when I take money out?
results.answer:
Yes. **Meeting the first-time home buyer test when you open an FHSA does not guarantee that you will meet the separate test for a tax-free qualifying withdrawal later.**

The tests look at different periods and, importantly, different ownership situations:

- **When opening the FHSA:** you must not have lived, in the current year before opening or the previous four calendar years, in a qualifying home that **you** owned—or that **your spouse/common-law partner at the time you open the FHSA** owned.
- **When making a qualifying withdrawal:** you must not have lived, in the current year before the withdrawal (other than the 30 days immediately before it) or the previous four calendar years, in a qualifying home that **you owned or jointly owned**.

So, for example, you could be eligible to open an FHSA and later become ineligible to make a qualifying withdrawal if you buy and live in a home before making the withdrawal. You must satisfy the withdrawal test **at the time of the withdrawal**, as well as the other qualifying-withdrawal conditions.

Those other conditions include giving your issuer Form RC725, having a written agreement to buy or build a qualifying home by the required deadline, being a Canadian resident during the applicable period, and intending to occupy the home as your principal residence within one year.

For a situation involving a spouse/common-law partner, a recent home purchase, or timing close to a withdrawal, consider confirming the facts with the CRA or a licensed tax professional.

results.question: What does the government guide explain about disability savings plans, government help, withdrawals, eligibility changes, and taxes?
results.answer:
A **registered disability savings plan (RDSP)** is a long-term savings plan for an individual approved for the **disability tax credit (DTC)**. It is structured as a trust arrangement with a Canadian trust company and is intended to support the beneficiary’s long-term financial security.

### Contributions and government help
- Contributions are **not tax-deductible**.
- Contributions can be made until the end of the year the beneficiary turns **59**.
- The government may deposit two types of assistance directly into the RDSP:

  **Canada Disability Savings Grant**
  - Matches contributions at **300%, 200%, or 100%**, depending on the beneficiary’s adjusted family net income and the amount contributed.
  - Maximum grant: **$3,500 per year** and **$70,000 over the beneficiary’s lifetime**.

  **Canada Disability Savings Bond**
  - For low-income Canadians with disabilities; **no contribution is required** to receive it.
  - Can be as much as **$1,000 per year**, with a **$20,000 lifetime maximum**.
  - Can be paid until the year the beneficiary turns **49**.
  - For **2025**, the full $1,000 bond is available at adjusted family net income of **$37,487 or less**; a partial bond may be available between **$37,487 and $57,375**. These thresholds are indexed annually.

To qualify for grants or bonds, the beneficiary must file income-tax and benefit returns for the prior two years and future years while they have an RDSP. For a beneficiary under 18, grant and bond calculations use the parents’ or guardians’ combined income from filed returns.

### Withdrawals and tax treatment
When money is paid from an RDSP:
- The original **contributions** withdrawn are **not taxable income** to the beneficiary.
- The following amounts **are taxable** to the beneficiary when withdrawn:
  - Canada Disability Savings Grants;
  - Canada Disability Savings Bonds;
  - investment income earned in the RDSP; and
  - proceeds from rollovers.

### Changes in disability-tax-credit eligibility
The supplied government material says an RDSP is intended for a person approved for the DTC, but it does **not** explain what happens if the beneficiary’s DTC eligibility later changes or ends. For that situation, the CRA or a qualified tax professional would be the appropriate source for case-specific guidance.

RDSPs, like other registered plans, are generally required to hold only **qualified investments**.
